page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 1 | Page 1 of 6

Lesson Overview: Portfolio Selection and Craft Rationale

Lesson Focus

Lesson 1: Portfolio Selection and Craft Rationale

Primary Standard: MLA.CW.WR.08 — Reflection on creative process and product.

Supporting Standards: MLA.CW.WR.09 — Portfolio selection and evidence; MLA.CW.REV.01 — Revision from feedback.

What You Will Learn

  • Choose portfolio pieces through evidence-based criteria.
  • Distinguish personal attachment from demonstrable craft quality.
  • Explain growth using precise draft-to-final evidence.
  • Write a defensible craft rationale for an unfamiliar audience.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 1 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task: Record every core term and its complete meaning in your notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context. Reference glossary terms do not need to be copied.
TermMeaningExample
craft rationaleAn evidence-based explanation of why a writer made or preserved particular artistic choices.The rationale connects the fragmented structure to the narrator’s uncertainty.
selection criterionA stated standard used to evaluate whether an item belongs in a collection.Range and revision depth are two portfolio selection criteria.
representativeAccurately showing an important quality, skill, or pattern.The scene is representative of the writer’s strongest dialogue.
rangeMeaningful variety in genre, purpose, technique, voice, or challenge.The portfolio shows range through poetry, fiction, and memoir.
artifactA work or piece of evidence included in a portfolio.A final story and its marked draft are separate artifacts.
revision evidenceSpecific before-and-after material showing how and why a work changed.Two excerpts document the pacing change and its effect.
metacognitionAwareness and analysis of one’s own thinking and decision-making.The reflection explains how the writer’s priorities changed.
tradeoffA gain in one quality that may require giving up or limiting another.Cutting a scene improves pace but reduces background detail.
defensible claimA conclusion supported by relevant reasons and evidence.The claim that the piece shows growth is supported by paired drafts.

Vocabulary in Action

Match each clue to the precise term. Choose Check, study any mismatch, and retry. This practice is ungraded.

Make the Vocabulary Work

Which statement is a defensible claim about portfolio selection?

A. “This is my best piece because I like it most.”

This states a preference without a criterion or evidence.

B. “This piece belongs because its two drafts show substantial pacing revisions and the final version demonstrates controlled tension.”

Correct. It applies criteria and supports the conclusion with revision evidence.

page.title: Lesson
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 1 | Page 3 of 6

Lesson: Select with Evidence, Explain with Precision

Step 1 — Define the Portfolio Purpose

Name what the portfolio must demonstrate: strongest current craft, growth across time, range, readiness for publication, or a combination. Selection criteria must follow that purpose.

Step 2 — Build an Evidence Matrix

CriterionEvidenceQuestion
Craft controlDiction, imagery, syntax, pacing, formWhere is the choice sustained?
GrowthBefore/after passage and feedbackWhat problem did revision solve?
RangeDifferent risks or techniquesWhat does this add that others do not?

Pause and Choose: Select by Criterion

A writer loves a personal poem, but another piece shows stronger craft control and a documented revision breakthrough. The portfolio’s main purpose is to demonstrate growth. Which choice is better supported?

A. Select the favorite poem because emotional attachment is enough evidence.
Weaker choice. Personal value can matter, but it does not demonstrate the stated criterion. The decision lacks observable evidence of growth.
B. Select the revised piece and document the problem, the before-and-after change, and the improvement it produced.
Stronger choice. This selection follows the portfolio purpose and gives specific evidence that an evaluator can examine.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Step 3 — Separate Preference from Judgment

Preference: “This is my favorite because it is personal.” Judgment: “This belongs because its recurring harbor image develops the speaker’s divided loyalty, and revision made that pattern structurally coherent.” Personal meaning may matter, but it is not sufficient evidence.

Step 4 — Write the Rationale

  1. Claim: name why the piece belongs.
  2. Craft evidence: quote or describe an exact decision.
  3. Revision evidence: compare a meaningful before-and-after change.
  4. Effect: explain what readers can perceive or experience.
  5. Portfolio contribution: show what the work adds to the collection.
  6. Limitation: acknowledge one remaining weakness or tradeoff.

Pause and Choose: Make the Rationale Specific

Which rationale is unmistakably tied to one artifact?

A. “This story belongs because moving the unopened letter from the ending to the first scene created a recurring choice that now drives the narrator’s conflict.”
Stronger choice. It identifies an exact revision, a structural function, and its effect on conflict. The claim could not simply be pasted onto any piece.
B. “This is one of my best pieces because I worked hard and improved it.”
Weaker choice. Effort and improvement are asserted but not demonstrated. The statement lacks a named decision, evidence, and reader effect.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Quality Test

Remove the title and ask whether the rationale could describe any piece. If yes, it is too vague. Add exact evidence until the reasoning is unmistakably tied to this artifact.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 1 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Three Selection Decisions

Example 1 — Strongest Piece vs. Strongest Growth

Poem A: polished imagery, little revision evidence. Poem B: slightly less polished, but feedback led the writer to replace abstract grief statements with a controlled pattern of empty-chair images.

  1. Purpose: demonstrate growth and craft reasoning.
  2. Evidence: B contains a traceable shift from abstraction to concrete motif.
  3. Effect: readers infer grief through pattern rather than explanation.
  4. Decision: select B, while acknowledging A may better represent current surface polish.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which portfolio choice best demonstrates growth and craft reasoning?

A. Select Poem A because the most polished piece always provides the strongest evidence of learning.
Weaker response. This assumes current polish is the only criterion and ignores the portfolio’s stated purpose of demonstrating growth.
B. Select Poem B because its revision trail shows abstract grief statements transformed into a controlled empty-chair motif, while acknowledging that Poem A has stronger surface polish.
Stronger response. This choice applies the purpose, cites traceable revision evidence, explains the reader effect, and acknowledges a legitimate tradeoff.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Example 2 — Avoiding Redundancy

Story C and Story D both use first-person narrators and withheld information. C controls revelation through scene order; D relies mainly on an unexplained final twist.

  1. Compare contribution: C demonstrates structural control; D repeats the same category less successfully.
  2. Select C for evidence of sustained technique.
  3. If D remains, revise it to demonstrate a genuinely different skill or genre.
  4. Rationale: selection must improve the portfolio as a system, not reward every acceptable piece.

Example 3 — Full Craft Rationale

Claim: “The Salt Line” belongs because it shows my growth in using setting as pressure rather than decoration.

Evidence: An early draft described the flooded road in one paragraph. The final version returns to the rising salt stain at each decision point.

Effect: The repeated measurement makes time and danger visible without a narrator explaining urgency.

Portfolio contribution: Unlike my dialogue-centered pieces, this story demonstrates structural imagery.

Limitation: The final scene still compresses the sibling’s reaction, so emotional consequence remains a next goal.

Transfer Formula

Portfolio purpose + exact craft evidence + revision evidence + reader effect + unique contribution + honest limitation = defensible selection.

Your Turn Before Independent Work

Pause and try: Choose one artifact for a growth portfolio: a flawless first draft or a strong revised draft with documented structural change. Defend the choice and name a limitation.

Check your thinking — open after you try
Teacher model: I would choose the revised draft because it demonstrates a deliberate structural decision and its effect. Its limitation may be slightly less sentence-level polish, which I would acknowledge rather than hide.

page.title: Independent Work
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 6 | Lesson 1 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Portfolio Selection and Craft Rationale

Purpose

Curate portfolio pieces using evidence of quality, range, purpose, and growth—not personal preference alone.

Complete each numbered part in your notebook. Support decisions with precise evidence from your portfolio work.

Source for Your Work

Selection challenge: Piece A is polished but shows a skill already represented twice. Piece B is less polished but demonstrates a major change in point of view and the writer’s strongest revision growth. Piece C is enjoyable but unfinished.

1. Plan Before You Work

Portfolio DecisionEvidence and Plan
Purpose and intended audienceState each precisely.
Strongest current evidenceName the piece, passage, or feature.
Most important improvementDescribe the needed change and intended effect.

2. Choose and Explain

Which approach demonstrates stronger author decision-making? Record A or B, then explain your choice in 2–3 sentences using a lesson concept.

A. Choose only the pieces with the highest grades because scores fully explain a writer’s range and growth.
B. Use clear criteria, compare evidence across pieces, and select work that creates a purposeful picture of craft and development.

3. Apply the Lesson

Evaluate four pieces from your course work using a selection matrix for quality, range, growth, and portfolio purpose. Select three and write a 100–150 word craft rationale for each using specific textual evidence.

4. Revise with Purpose

Challenge your weakest selection. Either replace it or strengthen its rationale with more precise evidence, then explain the decision.

Before You Submit

  • All four numbered parts are complete.
  • Your work applies the lesson skill to specific portfolio evidence.
  • Your explanation identifies a decision and its effect on the audience.
  • Your revision meaningfully improves quality, coherence, or readiness.
TOR Help

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Checkpoint: Portfolio Selection and Craft Rationale

Put the lesson together through analysis, decision-making, writing, and purposeful revision.

Purpose

Show that you can understand the lesson concept, apply it in original work, and explain your decisions. Complete every numbered item and submit your responses with your Checkpoint work.

New Source: The Selection Problem

A writer has room for three portfolio pieces: a technically clean early poem, a risky but uneven recent story, a revised scene that shows major growth, and a favorite monologue that repeats skills already shown elsewhere.

A craft rationale explains why a work belongs in a portfolio using evidence about purpose, technique, growth, and audience. Curation is purposeful selection and arrangement.

Part 1: Analyze the Source

  1. Which three pieces would create the strongest evidence of range and growth? Defend each selection with a different criterion.
  2. What revision would the risky recent story need before it could strengthen rather than weaken the collection?

Use this response pattern: Make a precise claim, cite the relevant detail, and explain how the detail proves the claim.

Part 2: Choose A or B

3. Which approach produces a defensible portfolio selection?

A. Select the three pieces the writer likes most and explain that each is meaningful.
B. Select pieces that collectively show quality, range, growth, and purposeful risk; support every claim with a specific feature of the work.

Record A or B in your submission and explain your choice in 2–3 sentences. The answer is not revealed here because this item is part of your graded written work.

Part 3: Create and Apply

4. Create a three-piece portfolio proposal using your own work.

  1. Portfolio purpose: State the audience and the impression the collection should create.
  2. Selection: Name three pieces in at least two forms and summarize each.
  3. Evidence: Cite one specific passage or craft feature from each piece.
  4. Rationale: Write 150–200 words per piece explaining quality, range, growth, and contribution to the whole.
  5. Sequence: Arrange the pieces and explain how the order guides the reader.

Plan before drafting: Decide what the audience should understand, how each section will build that understanding, and which details will do the most work.

Part 4: Revise With Purpose

5. Replace one preference-based claim such as “I like this” with a precise claim supported by craft evidence.

Do more than correct spelling. Revise organization, meaning, evidence, or craft so the work becomes clearer and more effective.

Before You Submit

  • Every numbered item is complete.
  • Analysis includes specific evidence and reasoning.
  • The creative work follows the required organization and length.
  • The A/B response is recorded and explained.
  • The revision is visible and its purpose is clear.

Mastery Target

A score of 80% or higher demonstrates mastery. Depth, control, and application matter more than unnecessary length.

TOR Help

If you are unsure how to organize your response, choose evidence, or revise meaningfully, contact your Teacher of Record before submitting.
